arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Lisa Madigan argued the sniff is not a search. She cited Place and Edmond as precedent for this view.
Robert Wray stated the stop was lawful. He noted the stop lasted less than nine minutes.
Michael Meczyk argued the state lacked justification. He claimed the sniff invaded Cabales' Fourth Amendment interests.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether a drug dog sniff during a lawful traffic stop counts as a Fourth Amendment search. Illinois claims the sniff needs no justification. Cabales claims the sniff violated his privacy rights.

paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 10, 2004.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Illinois wants the Court to rule the dog sniff is not a search. This would let police use dogs freely during traffic stops.
Cabales wants the Court to rule the dog sniff is a search. This would require police to have a valid reason before using a dog.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Illinois argues a dog sniff is not a search. They cite prior cases saying sniffs need no Fourth Amendment justification.
Cabales argues the sniff invaded his privacy. He says the state offered no valid Fourth Amendment justification for the action.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Stevens asked if officers knew Cabales in advance. He noted they do not arrest every speeding driver.
Justice Kennedy asked if the location mattered more than the target. He questioned the nature of the place searched.
